q: In a dwelling-unit living room, wall receptacles must be placed so that no point measured horizontally along the floor line of any wall space is more than how far from a receptacle?
explain: The 6-ft rule — which produces the familiar 12-ft maximum spacing between receptacles. Wall spaces 2 ft or wider count.

q: For kitchen wall countertop spaces, receptacles must be installed so no point along the wall line is more than how far from a receptacle?
explain: 24 in. — so countertop receptacles are at most 4 ft apart. Any wall counter space 12 in. or wider needs one.

q: Which dwelling-unit receptacle location does NOT require GFCI protection under 210.8(A)?
explain: 210.8(A) lists bathrooms, garages, outdoors, crawl spaces, basements, kitchens (countertop-serving), within 6 ft of sinks, boathouses, near bathtubs/showers, and laundry areas. Ordinary living areas are not on the list.

q: In a dwelling, 125 V receptacles installed within what distance of the top inside edge of a sink bowl require GFCI protection?
explain: Within 6 ft of the sink, measured from the top inside edge of the bowl.

q: A dwelling unit kitchen requires a minimum of how many 20-ampere small-appliance branch circuits?
explain: At least two 20 A small-appliance circuits serving the kitchen, pantry, dining and similar areas' receptacles.

q: The dwelling-unit bathroom receptacle branch circuit must be rated at least:
explain: At least one 20 A circuit for bathroom receptacles, with no other outlets unless it serves a single bathroom.

q: Which dwelling-unit area is NOT listed as requiring AFCI protection for its 120 V, 15 and 20 A branch circuits?
explain: 210.12(A) covers kitchens, family/dining/living rooms, bedrooms, closets, hallways, laundry areas and similar. Bathrooms, garages and outdoors are not listed.

q: A branch circuit supplies 40 A of continuous load and no noncontinuous load. The overcurrent device must be rated at least:
explain: Continuous load × 125% = 50 A. Conductors (210.19(A)) follow the same 125% rule before adjustment.

q: A 20 A branch circuit supplies two or more receptacles. What receptacle ratings are permitted?
explain: 15 A circuit → 15 A receptacles only (not more than 15); 20 A circuit → 15 or 20 A; 30 A → 30 A; 40 A → 40 or 50 A; 50 A → 50 A.

q: On a branch circuit supplying two or more outlets, cord-and-plug-connected utilization equipment not fastened in place shall not exceed what percentage of the circuit rating?
explain: 80% of the branch-circuit ampere rating for portable cord-and-plug equipment.

q: A dwelling-unit hallway requires at least one receptacle outlet when it is at least how long?
explain: Hallways 10 ft or more in length, measured along the centerline without passing through a doorway.

q: One- and two-family dwellings need outdoor receptacles accessible at grade level at the front and back, installed not more than how high above grade?
explain: Not more than 6½ ft (2.0 m) above grade. Garage receptacles use 5½ ft.

q: In an attached dwelling garage, at least one receptacle is required in each vehicle bay, installed not more than how high above the floor?
explain: Not more than 5½ ft (1.7 m) above the floor, one per vehicle bay.

q: In a dwelling, at least one wall-switch-controlled lighting outlet is required in:
choices: Every habitable room, kitchen, and bathroom
explain: Every habitable room, kitchen and bathroom. In rooms other than kitchens and bathrooms, a switched receptacle can substitute.

q: The general lighting load for a dwelling unit is calculated at how many volt-amperes per square foot?
explain: 3 VA/ft² of floor area (not counting open porches, garages, or unused/unfinished spaces not adaptable for future use).

q: In a standard dwelling load calculation, each small-appliance circuit and the laundry circuit are each counted at:
explain: 1,500 VA each — so two small-appliance circuits plus laundry add 4,500 VA before demand factors.

q: A 2,000 sq ft dwelling has two small-appliance circuits and one laundry circuit. Using the standard method, what is the general lighting and receptacle demand load?
For a household electric clothes dryer, the load used in the calculation is:
choices: 5,000 W or the nameplate rating, whichever is larger
explain: 5,000 W or nameplate, whichever is larger. Demand factors in Table 220.54 apply for 5 or more dryers.

q: Using Table 220.55 Column C, the demand load for one household range rated 12 kW is:
explain: Column C allows 8 kW for one range rated not over 12 kW. Over 12 kW, add 5% per kW above 12.

q: In other than dwelling units, each general-use receptacle outlet is calculated at:
explain: 180 VA per yoke/strap (a 4-plex counts at 360 VA).

q: The service disconnecting means shall be installed at a readily accessible location:
choices: Either outside the building or inside nearest the point of entrance of the service conductors
In the same room as the meter
explain: Outside, or inside nearest the point of entrance of the service conductors — not in a bathroom (230.70(A)(2)).

q: The maximum number of service disconnecting means permitted for each service is:
explain: Up to six, and in the 2020 edition each must be in a separate enclosure or compartment (230.71(B)).

q: The service disconnecting means for a one-family dwelling must have a rating of not less than:
explain: 100 A, 3-wire minimum for a one-family dwelling. Other installations: 60 A general; 30 A for limited loads of a single branch circuit; 15 A for one 2-wire circuit.

q: Overhead service conductors (not over 300 V to ground) passing over a residential driveway must have a minimum vertical clearance of:
explain: 12 ft over residential property and driveways; 10 ft above finished grade at the service entrance (≤150 V to ground); 18 ft over public streets and parking areas subject to truck traffic.

q: Service conductors installed as open conductors or multiconductor cable without an overall jacket must have a clearance of at least how much from windows designed to be opened?
explain: 3 ft from windows, doors, porches, balconies, fire escapes. Conductors run above the top level of a window are exempt.

q: The maximum standard overcurrent device rating for 12 AWG copper conductors (absent a specific exception) is:
explain: Small-conductor rule: 14 AWG Cu → 15 A, 12 AWG Cu → 20 A, 10 AWG Cu → 30 A (12 AWG Al → 15 A, 10 AWG Al → 25 A).

q: Which of the following is NOT a standard ampere rating for fuses and inverse-time circuit breakers?
A feeder conductor has an adjusted ampacity of 65 A and does not supply a multioutlet receptacle circuit. The largest standard overcurrent device permitted is:
explain: Next-size-up rule: when ampacity doesn't match a standard rating and the device is 800 A or less, the next higher standard rating (70 A) is permitted.

q: Under the 25-ft feeder tap rule, the tap conductors must have an ampacity of at least:
choices: One-tenth of the feeder OCPD rating
One-third of the feeder OCPD rating
One-half of the feeder OCPD rating
explain: 25-ft tap: at least 1/3 of the feeder overcurrent device rating, terminating in a single OCPD, protected from damage. 10-ft tap has its own conditions.

q: Overcurrent devices shall be readily accessible and installed so the center of the operating handle, in its highest position, is not more than how far above the floor?
explain: 6 ft 7 in. (2.0 m), with exceptions such as busways and devices adjacent to the equipment they supply.

q: In dwelling units, overcurrent devices (other than supplementary protection) shall NOT be located in:
explain: Not in bathrooms of dwellings or guest rooms, and not in the vicinity of easily ignitable material such as clothes closets (240.24(D)).

q: The portion of a grounding electrode conductor that is the sole connection to a ground rod is not required to be larger than:
explain: Rod, pipe or plate electrodes: 6 AWG Cu max. Concrete-encased electrode: 4 AWG Cu max (250.66(B)). Ground ring: no larger than the ring conductor.

q: A single ground rod electrode must be supplemented by an additional electrode unless it has a resistance to earth of:
explain: 25 ohms or less, otherwise add a second electrode spaced at least 6 ft away (250.53(A)(3)).

q: When two ground rods are installed, they must be spaced at least how far apart?
explain: Not less than 6 ft (1.8 m) apart. Rods must be at least 8 ft long and driven their full length (250.52(A)(5), 250.53(G)).

q: A concrete-encased electrode (Ufer) requires at least how much electrically conductive steel reinforcing bar of ½-in. minimum diameter?
explain: At least 20 ft of ½-in. rebar, or 20 ft of bare 4 AWG copper, encased in at least 2 in. of concrete in direct contact with earth.

q: A 100 A circuit requires a copper equipment grounding conductor of at least what size?
On the load side of the service disconnecting means, the grounded (neutral) conductor:
choices: Must be bonded to every panel enclosure
Shall not be connected to equipment grounding conductors or enclosures
May be used as the equipment ground for ranges
Must be re-grounded at each subpanel
explain: The neutral-to-ground bond happens once, at the service. Downstream, neutrals and EGCs stay separate so no neutral current flows on metal parts.

q: A feeder supplies a detached garage from a dwelling. At the garage panel, the grounded conductor:
choices: Is bonded to the enclosure and grounding electrode
Is kept isolated from the EGC and enclosure; an EGC is run with the feeder
explain: Run an equipment grounding conductor with the feeder and keep the neutral isolated at the second building. A grounding electrode is still required there (250.32(A)).

q: The bonding jumper for a building's metal water piping system supplied by a service is sized according to:
choices: Table 250.122 based on the largest OCPD
Table 250.102(C)(1) based on the service conductors
explain: Sized from the service-entrance conductors using Table 250.102(C)(1), and in the 2020 edition it need not be larger than 3/0 copper or 250 kcmil aluminum. (The 2017 edition pointed to this table too; earlier editions used Table 250.66.)

q: Which raceway is recognized as an equipment grounding conductor without added conditions on length or fitting type?
explain: RMC, IMC and EMT are EGCs by themselves. FMC and LFMC qualify only with listed fittings, limited OCPD size and a 6-ft total length limit. Nonmetallic raceways never qualify.

q: An insulated equipment grounding conductor shall be identified by:
choices: Green, or green with one or more yellow stripes
explain: Green or green with yellow stripes, or bare. White/gray is reserved for the grounded conductor (200.6).

q: An insulated grounded (neutral) conductor 6 AWG or smaller shall be identified by:
choices: A continuous white or gray outer finish, or three continuous white or gray stripes
explain: White, gray, or three continuous white/gray stripes on other than green insulation.

q: An 8 AWG copper grounding electrode conductor run along a surface must be:
choices: Protected in rigid metal conduit, IMC, PVC, RTRC, EMT, or cable armor
explain: GECs smaller than 6 AWG need raceway or armor protection. 6 AWG may be exposed along the structure if not subject to physical damage; 4 AWG and larger may be exposed.

q: A service has 500 kcmil copper service-entrance conductors. The minimum copper main bonding jumper is:
explain: Table 250.102(C)(1): over 350 through 600 kcmil copper → 1/0 AWG copper. Above 1,100 kcmil, use 12½% of the largest phase conductor area.

q: Each multiwire branch circuit must be provided with a means to:
choices: Simultaneously disconnect all ungrounded conductors at the point where the circuit originates
explain: A multipole breaker or handle-tied single poles at the panel. Conductors of a multiwire circuit must also be grouped (210.4(D)).

q: A feeder supplies 60 A of continuous load and 40 A of noncontinuous load. Before any adjustment or correction, the minimum feeder conductor ampacity is:
explain: (60 × 1.25) + 40 = 75 + 40 = 115 A. The OCPD follows the same math (215.3).

q: Using the optional method for a dwelling unit, the general loads are taken at 100% for the first 10 kVA and at what percentage for the remainder?
explain: 100% of the first 10 kVA, 40% of the rest; then add the larger of the heating or cooling loads per 220.82(C).

q: Service conductors are considered 'outside' a building when installed:
choices: Inside a metal raceway anywhere in the building
Beneath at least 2 in. of concrete under the building
Within 10 ft of the exterior wall
explain: 230.6 lists: under 2 in. of concrete beneath the building, within the building in 2 in. of concrete/brick, in a vault, in conduit under 18 in. of earth under the building, etc.

q: If a metal underground water pipe, a concrete-encased electrode, and a ground rod are all present at a building, which must be bonded together to form the grounding electrode system?
choices: All electrodes present must be bonded together
explain: All grounding electrodes described in 250.52(A)(1) through (A)(7) that are present must be bonded together. Metal water pipe must also be supplemented (250.53(D)(2)).

q: The two small-appliance branch circuits in a dwelling kitchen may supply:
choices: Receptacles in the kitchen, pantry, breakfast room and dining room, plus refrigeration equipment
explain: Receptacle outlets in the kitchen and dining-type areas (including the refrigerator, which may also have its own 15 A+ circuit). No lighting or other outlets.

q: When ungrounded conductors are increased in size to compensate for voltage drop, the equipment grounding conductor:
choices: Must be increased proportionately by circular-mil area
Can be omitted if the raceway is metal
explain: Wire-type EGCs are upsized in proportion to the increase in the ungrounded conductors' circular-mil area.

q: Generally, a building or structure served by a feeder from another building shall be supplied by:
choices: Only one feeder or branch circuit
explain: One supply per building unless a 225.30 exception applies (special conditions, different voltages, capacity, etc.) — parallel to the one-service rule in 230.2.
